content: Gibbsite, chemically represented as Al(OH)₃, is one of the mineral forms of aluminum hydroxide. It is commonly referred to as γ-Al(OH)₃, though it is sometimes designated as α-Al(OH)₃. Another name for gibbsite is hydrargillite (or hydrargyllite). This mineral is a significant source of aluminum, as it constitutes one of the three primary phases found in bauxite, a rock that serves as the principal ore of aluminum. While bauxite is often mistaken for a single mineral, it is actually a composite rock made up of hydroxide and oxyhydroxide minerals such as gibbsite, boehmite (γ-AlO(OH)), and diaspore (α-AlO(OH)), along with clays, silt, and iron oxides and hydroxides. Gibbsite has three recognized structural polymorphs or polytypes: bayerite (commonly designated as α-Al(OH)₃, though sometimes referred to as β-Al(OH)₃), doyleite, and nordstrandite. Both gibbsite and bayerite exhibit monoclinic crystal structures, whereas doyleite and nordstrandite are triclinic in form. The structure of gibbsite is particularly noteworthy and bears resemblance to the fundamental structure of micas. Its basic framework consists of stacked sheets of interconnected octahedra formed by aluminum hydroxide. Each octahedron is composed of an aluminum ion with a +3 charge, coordinated to six hydroxide ions, each carrying a -1 charge. Notably, one-third of the octahedra lack a central aluminum ion, resulting in hydroxides that are bonded to only two aluminum atoms. This arrangement creates a neutral sheet, as the charges balance out: the +3 charge of aluminum is distributed across six hydroxide bonds, yielding a +1/2 charge per bond, while the -1 charge of each hydroxide is shared between two aluminum atoms, resulting in a -1/2 charge. The neutrality of these sheets means there is no electrostatic charge to attract ions between the layers, which could otherwise act as a glue to hold the sheets together. Consequently, the sheets are only weakly bonded by residual forces, making gibbsite a soft mineral that is easily cleaved. The structural similarity between gibbsite and brucite (Mg(OH)₂) is also of interest. However, the lower charge of magnesium (+2) in brucite, compared to aluminum (+3) in gibbsite, eliminates the need for one-third of the octahedra to be vacant in brucite to maintain a neutral sheet. The differing symmetries of gibbsite and brucite arise from variations in the stacking arrangements of their layers. Gibbsite's layers serve as a structural precursor to the mineral corundum (Al₂O₃). The basic structure of corundum is nearly identical to that of gibbsite, except that the hydroxide ions in gibbsite are replaced by oxygen ions in corundum. Since oxygen carries a -2 charge, the layers in corundum are not neutral and must bond with additional aluminum atoms above and below the initial layer. This bonding creates the three-dimensional framework characteristic of corundum's structure. Gibbsite is also notable for its role in the structure of other minerals. Its neutral aluminum hydroxide sheets are often found sandwiched between silicate sheets in important clay mineral groups, such as illite, kaolinite, and montmorillonite/smectite. These individual aluminum hydroxide layers are identical to those in gibbsite and are referred to as gibbsite layers. The mineral gibbsite is named after George Gibbs (1776–1833), an American mineral collector. His extensive collection was acquired by Yale University in the early 19th century.
